finding.new: Non-discriminating: eclipse magnetic effects follow from the ionospheric Sq current system (an effect Chapman worked out for the ionospheric current system in 1933, confirmed statistically across INTERMAGNET by Kim & Chang 2018) without dome geometry. The dome's station-to-station factor (FSF) follows from its flat Polaris-triangulation equation and equals the ratio of tan(latitude); its exponential height function plays no role. The absolute magnitude is imported from the 2017 Boulder observation, which the dome has since withdrawn as 'storm contamination' while still calibrating its 2026 predictions from it. Planetary Kp during the 2017 eclipse was 1+ to 2o, far below storm level, and, on the dome's own measure (lowest Z in the eclipse window minus the previous day's mean), the other 29 days of August 2017 give a median of −19.9 nT, with 16 of them reaching −18.22 nT or lower — the eclipse day is ordinary.

detail_claim.new: Boulder (BOU) INTERMAGNET station observed a −10.9 nT anomaly at 17:20 UTC during the 2017 Aug 21 solar eclipse, described by the dome as coincident with eclipse maximum. (Boulder's eclipse maximum was at ≈17:46 UTC, about 26 minutes later.) The dome's wins.html now cites the 2016-03-09 Pacific eclipse for WIN-010 instead. Its AI Context Archive page still lists WIN-010 as the 2017 Boulder result (“-10.9 nT at 17:20 UTC. Tracks geometry not time.”), while its PROS-003 audit on wins.html says the 2017 minima did not track eclipse geometry. The dome's pages take three different positions on this one WIN.

detail_evidence.new:
Eclipse-induced magnetic perturbations follow from the ionospheric Sq current system. Chapman (1919, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 218:1–118) described the solar-driven daily variation. Chapman (1933, “The effect of a solar eclipse on the Earth's magnetic field”, Terr. Magn. Atmos. Electr. 38:175–183) worked out what an eclipse should do to that current system if it flows in the E-layer, and then judged that the eclipse records available in 1933 did not show the predicted effect; he left the question to further observations. During an eclipse the Moon's shadow cuts ionizing UV, E-region conductivity falls, and the Sq current weakens locally; the modern conductivity treatment is Yamazaki & Maute (2017, Space Science Reviews 206:299–405). The confirmation came later: Kim & Chang (2018, Advances in Space Research 61:2040–2049), analysing roughly 200 records from 100 INTERMAGNET observatories over 1991–2016, find that the effect grows with eclipse magnitude and is most conspicuous at magnetic latitudes of 30°–50°. Boulder sits inside that band (≈48° by either the centered-dipole or AACGM convention). Which way each field component moves depends on where a station sits relative to the shadow, so the effect is not a uniform dip.

What Boulder recorded in 2017. The published analysis of this event at Boulder that we found, Meza et al. (2022) (Advances in Space Research 69:16–25), compares the eclipse day with the mean of five nearby quiet days after 15-minute smoothing and removing a linear trend over two hours centred on maximum (read in the arXiv preprint, 2107.12327). It finds the eclipse signature mainly in the northward (X) component, about +10 nT near maximum, with the vertical (Z) component small and positive, a few nT, and a thin-current-sheet model driven by the measured drop in ionospheric electron content reproduces both (values read from their Figure 7). We repeated the Z check on INTERMAGNET definitive minute data. Relative to the mean of the five quietest days of 10–31 August 2017 at the same time of day (aligned on the hour before the eclipse began), Boulder's Z was +0.8 nT at the dome's 17:20 UTC and +4.9 nT at eclipse maximum — but a single-minute value at one station carries roughly ±8 nT of day-to-day noise (a leave-one-out null on the same five days gives Z at 17:20 ranging from −1.2 to +9.6 nT, population sd 8.6 nT; an alternative five-day set gives sd 7.7 nT), and the choice of alignment (pre-eclipse hour / night / daily mean / none) moves the 17:20 value between −3.8 and +1.1 nT, while the eclipse-maximum value stays positive (+0.3 to +4.9 nT) under every alignment and quiet-day-set variant tried. Across these variants, eclipse-day Z at 17:20 lies between −3.8 and +1.1 nT and at maximum between +0.3 and +4.9 nT — never near the dome's −10.9 nT — but Boulder's Z alone cannot confirm or exclude a roughly 10 nT effect, because quiet days differ from each other by about ±8 nT at a single minute. Standard physics therefore accounts for an eclipse effect at Boulder, but that effect is not a −10.9 nT drop in Z. The dome's figures come from its choice of baseline. It does not say which baseline gives −10.9 nT. Its re-audit (OPEN-009 on model.html) compares the lowest Z in the eclipse window with the 20 August daily mean and reports −18.22 nT, with “Range −16.38 to −23.38 nT depending on baseline window.” We reproduce −18.22 nT exactly; the minimum falls at 19:07 UTC, 81 minutes after eclipse maximum and seven minutes before the eclipse ended. On the dome's own measure (lowest Z in the eclipse window minus the previous day's mean), the five quiet days give −26.2, −29.1, −7.7, −7.4, and −7.7 nT (range −7.4 to −29.1 nT); across all 29 non-eclipse days of 2–31 August 2017 the median is −19.9 nT, and 16 of them reach −18.22 nT or lower — the eclipse day sits at about the 45th percentile and is ordinary, because Boulder's Z normally reaches its daily low in that part of the day. (Script, input checksums and output: monitor/analyst/analysis-records/win010-c17-rev2-verification-20260929.json.) We have not run a multi-station timing analysis of the 2017 event and do not claim one: the dome's minimum at 17:20 UTC sits about 26 minutes before Boulder's eclipse maximum (≈17:46 UTC; timeanddate.com local circumstances, magnitude 0.940; our JPL DE440s run gives 17:46 UTC and 93.7%), and the dome's own later audit says its 2017 minima did not track eclipse timing (see below). The dome has no equation that derives eclipse magnitudes from dome parameters; it observes a number and counts it as a WIN.

Kp record (corrected 2026-09-27). Earlier versions of this entry said the 2017 observation “was recorded at Kp ≈ 3” and called 2016-03-09 “a genuinely Kp<2 quiet day.” Both statements were wrong, and we are correcting them against the same source we use to audit the dome in WIN-025: the GFZ Potsdam definitive Kp record (kp.gfz.de; responses archived in monitor/analyst/analysis-records/win010-c16-verification-snapshots-20260927.json). For the 3-hour slots covering each eclipse: 2016-03-09 (Guam eclipse 00:22–03:24 UTC, maximum 01:52): Kp 2o at 00–03 UTC and 2− at 03–06 UTC; 2o is at the dome's threshold rather than below it. 2017-08-21 (Boulder eclipse 16:23–19:14 UTC, maximum ≈17:46, dome minimum 17:20): Kp 1+ in the 15–18 UTC slot and 2o in the 18–21 UTC slot. The day's peak of Kp 3o fell at 06–09 UTC, about ten hours before the eclipse. 2024-04-08 (North American eclipse; see WIN-025): Kp 1+ at 15–18 UTC and 0+ at 18–21 UTC. None of the three days came near storm level (NOAA's G1 threshold is Kp 5): every eclipse-window slot was at Kp 2o or below. The differences between the three events are a third to two-thirds of a Kp unit, too small to rank them, and they give no support to the dome's label of 2017 and 2024 as “storm-contaminated.” By the dome's own Kp < 2 test, the second half of the 2017 window (2o) fails, and so does the first slot of the 2016 window (2o), the day the dome calls “the quietest eclipse day on record.”

What the dome gets right here: its model page correctly notes that 2017-08-21 was “geomagnetically disturbed pre-eclipse” (the morning Kp 3o), and it ranks events by local Boulder variability (standard deviation 2.23 nT in 2016, 8.05 nT in 2017, 5.59 nT in 2024 per the live wins.html WIN-010 entry). Local variance is a reasonable detectability measure. Its storm label, however, finds no support in Kp, and the dome does not say over which window the variance was computed. If that window is the eclipse itself, the ranking is confounded by local time. The 2016 eclipse fell at 17:22–20:24 MST in Boulder (evening of 8 March, local date). The Sun was 6.5° up at the start and set at about 18:01 MST, so most of that window was after dark, when Sq variation is weak. The 2017 and 2024 eclipses both fell near Boulder's local noon, when Sq variation and any eclipse effect are largest. A midday eclipse raises Boulder's variance on its own; that is not storm contamination. (This local-time reading is our inference and has not been checked against the dome's unstated window.)

The dome's monitor.py carries a “Kp < 2 required for eclipse signal” label (domain #12), but it only logs the latest real-time NOAA Kp value; it does not gate or score any eclipse result. The Kp < 2 precondition lives on the dome's predictions page (“Eclipse predictions valid only if Kp < 2 on August 12, 2026”; Tier 3: “Kp < 2 entire Aug 9–12 window”; and, for the registered Ebro figure PRED-095, “Requires Kp<2 within 3 hours of totality”). What happened when that condition was tested on 12 August 2026 is covered in the post-event status in the verdict text.

The station scaling (FSF). The dome's 2026 predictions multiply a baseline by each station's coverage and a “field strength factor” (FSF) it attributes to “V12 H(r)/r dome geometry.” Solving the dome's V12 equation r·tan(θ) = 8537·exp(−r/8619) for each station's latitude and normalizing to Boulder reproduces all nine published FSF values (0.642–2.075) to within 0.6% at seven stations and 2.78% at the worst (Pearson r = 0.9999). But V12 is r·tan(θ) = H(r) with θ set equal to geographic latitude, so H(r)/r = tan(latitude) at every station and FSFi = tan(lati)/tan(latBOU) exactly, whatever H(r) is. Pure tan(lat)/tan(40.015°) matches the published table at r = 0.999915, with seven of nine stations within 0.1%. The genuine dome content in the FSF is V12 itself, the flat-geometry Polaris triangulation. The exponential H(r) and its 8537/8619 km constants contribute nothing; the published table can be reproduced with a calculator from station latitudes alone.

The magnitude is imported, and the dome has disowned its source. The scaling does not supply the Boulder magnitude. The dome's 2026-03-12 table used the 2017 BOU value (−10.9 nT) as its baseline. Its model page later re-audited the same 2017 event at −18.22 nT against a 2017-08-20 quiet-day baseline (OPEN-009, model.html) and told readers to multiply every BOU-column prediction by 1.672 (= 18.22/10.9). Meanwhile PROS-003 on wins.html (status dated 2026-03-15) says: “Timing audit shows Z minima uncorrelated with eclipse geometry across 2017 and 2024 events (scatter −180 to +111 min from totality). Anomalies attributed to geomagnetic storm contamination, not eclipse signal.” The dome removed the 2017 event as evidence but kept it as the calibration for its only prospective eclipse prediction, as the numerator of WIN-012's coupling constant (monitor.py domain #7: kappa_obs = 10.9 / 6.5), and as the −18.22 nT baseline in its automated eclipse scoring (monitor.py domain #10).

Dome-side update (verified 2026-07-19, re-checked 2026-09-27). The live site now titles this entry “WIN-010 — Eclipse Magnetic Signal Confirmed on Quiet Days” and rests it on the 2016-03-09 Pacific total eclipse: GUA −13.16 nT (SNR 4.85), Z-component minima within 30 minutes of totality at five stations (GUA −3, HON +15, MMB +17, CNB −10, GNG +9 min) and H-component tracking at three (MMB −19, CNB +6, ASP −25 min). Multi-station timing coherence within about ±25 minutes of totality is real and worth having, and it is exactly what the Sq framework predicts for a sunlit ionosphere under the shadow. It does not discriminate between the dome and standard physics. The same holds for the confirmed nine-station 2024 North American cohort in WIN-025 (Chernogor & Holub, 2024). Verdict unchanged: Std Model Explains.

detail_verdict_text.new:
Non-discriminating. The Sq current framework (Chapman 1919; first applied to eclipses by Chapman 1933, who found the observations of his day inconclusive; Yamazaki & Maute 2017) predicts eclipse-correlated magnetic perturbations without any dome parameter, and Kim & Chang (2018, Adv. Space Res. 61:2040–2049) confirm statistically across INTERMAGNET that the effect scales with eclipse magnitude and is strongest at magnetic latitudes 30°–50°. The dome's own predictions page concedes the point. Its Tier 1 block is headed “Magnetic Signal (Globe-Compatible)” and gives the globe prediction as “0.0 nT systematic (or ionospheric Sq disruption — competing mechanism exists, see WIN-068 honest caveat)” (predictions.html), while its WIN-010 entry says “Globe has no mechanism predicting eclipse-correlated magnetic anomalies.” Those two dome pages contradict each other, and the first one agrees with this verdict.

The magnitude is borrowed, then reused. The dome's formula ΔZ = baseline × coverage × FSF takes its magnitude from observation. The 2017 Boulder value served as a confirmed WIN, as WIN-012's coupling-constant numerator (κ = 10.9/6.5), and as the 2026 baseline. Training data cannot also be test data. The 2026-03-12 table added a second anchor, the Mohe 1997 “W004 empirical” value of −22.24 nT (the event behind WIN-014, which our review rates Refuted by Data), giving two prediction columns about a factor of two apart at every station (10.9/22.24 = 0.490). Almost any post-eclipse value sits nearer one column than the other, which invites choosing the anchor after the fact. The dome has published at least five different Ebro figures for the same event: −10.7 nT (BOU column) and −21.7 nT (W004 column) on 2026-03-12; −17.8 nT ±2 nT in the registered claim PRED-095 (2026-04-04), whose printed formula −18.22 × 0.978 × (1 − 0.022) actually gives −17.4 nT because the (1 − 0.022) factor is printed but not applied; “−17 to −21 nT at stations with >80% coverage” on the predictions page; and −28.9 nT in its automated scoring. The last comes from monitor.py computing −18.22 × 0.95 × 1.672. The 1.672 sits in the slot where Ebro's FSF (1.029) belongs, and it equals the OPEN-009 re-audit ratio (18.22/10.9 = 1.672; OPEN-009 itself says “Multiply … by 1.67”), which −18.22 already contains, so the correction appears twice. The code does not say whether that is intended, and the dome's predictions page also equates the number with its coupling constant (“correction factor 1.672 = κ = 1.67 nT/µGal to 3 decimal places”). Kill Shots Test 5 tracks the same spread.

What we grant on the scaling. The FSF is dome geometry. It follows from V12, the flat Polaris triangulation r·tan(θ) = H(r), which makes FSF = tan(lat)/tan(latBOU). The part the dome presents as its derivation, the exponential H(r) with its 8537/8619 km constants, drops out and contributes nothing (details in the evidence panel; WIN-044 covers the dome's separate three-constant FSF(lat) fit). A correct ratio between stations still does not predict the signal. Section 1.8 (The Coordinate Collapse) adds that the disc radii feeding V12 come from Polaris elevations that pass through the same n(r) medium the dome says is 300–6,000× more refractive than Earth's atmosphere.

The Kp argument, corrected. An earlier version of this verdict argued that the dome accepted a Kp ≈ 3 observation as a WIN while demanding Kp < 2 for future tests. The GFZ definitive record does not support that. The 2017 eclipse ran at Kp 1+ to 2o (the Kp 3o came ten hours earlier), and the 2016 replacement ran at Kp 2o then 2− (figures and sources in the evidence panel). We withdraw the asymmetric-standard argument. What the record does show is that none of the three eclipses the dome cites came near storm level: every eclipse-window slot was at Kp 2o or below, against NOAA's G1 threshold of Kp 5. The planetary record gives no support to the dome's label of 2017 as storm-contaminated, and the differences between the events are too small to rank them. Yet the dome withdrew the 2017 event on storm grounds (PROS-003, 2026-03-15) and kept it as the calibration for every 2026 prediction (OPEN-009 on model.html; monitor.py domains #7 and #10). The dome's re-audit uses 20 August 2017 as its “quiet-day” baseline because 21 August was disturbed before the eclipse; on the GFZ record 20 August itself reached Kp 5o (G1 storm level) with Ap 20, against a peak of 3o and Ap 9 on the eclipse day. Either the 2017 event is contaminated, in which case the dome's 2026 magnitudes and WIN-012's κ rest on a contaminated number, or it is sound, in which case the withdrawal was wrong. The dome cannot have both. This argument does not depend on any of our physics. Our Boulder check (evidence panel) points to a third reading: the −18.22 nT figure is what an ordinary quiet afternoon at Boulder gives on the dome's measure, so it is unusable as a calibration whether or not 2017 was disturbed.

Post-hoc test. Independent of the physics, this claim fails our post-hoc test. The confirming values come from public INTERMAGNET archives that predate the dome's 2026 registrations (live WIN-010: “Registered: Originally 2026-03-06 | Audited: 2026-03-15”), and we found no pre-registration of the expected value in a timestamping venue independent of the author. Under the dome author's own definition (“prediction was timestamped before confirming data was pulled”), temporal ordering cannot be established from the repository history.

The 2026-08-12 test as we pre-registered it, and its limits. Before the eclipse we pre-registered a comparison of per-station residuals, (observed ΔZ) / (baseline × coverage), against two profiles: the dome's FSF (tan of geographic latitude) and a magnetic-latitude profile based on Kim & Chang's 30°–50° band. Stations inside the band were expected to carry an ensemble-median signal. Stations outside it were expected to fall to ≤30% of the in-band median, a first-order bound adopted because the paper does not tabulate the out-of-band drop-off. That gave a crude but falsifiable nine-number competitor to the dome's nine FSF numbers. We also pre-registered a coverage-exponent sensitivity check: divide observed ΔZ by baseline × coverageα for α ∈ {0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5}. If the ranking of the two profiles holds across that range, the linear-coverage approximation is adequate; if it flips, neither profile can claim the result. The frozen registration is predictions/eclipse-2026-08-12-predictions.json (OpenTimestamps-anchored 2026-05-02). The evaluation must report four limitations that were not handled in advance. We are stating them now, before any residuals are published. (1) Coverage inputs. The pre-registration did not say whose coverage values the residual uses. The dome's per-station “coverage” figures are far below ephemeris obscuration at the northern stations: Niemegk 40% vs about 85%, Lerwick 42% vs 88%, Eskdalemuir 55% vs 91%, Chambon 70% vs 93%, Hartland 80% vs 94% (JPL DE421 ephemeris; Hartland confirmed independently, see below). The ratio reaches about ×2.1 at Niemegk and Lerwick and correlates with FSF (r ≈ 0.84). A residual built on the dome's coverage would therefore inflate exactly where FSF predicts larger values. The evaluation will report both versions and label the ephemeris version as post-hoc. Separately, the dome's per-station predictions fail on geometry inputs alone, whatever the magnetometers show. (2) Solar elevation. The Sun stood only 3°–14° above the horizon at eclipse maximum at every European station, against 57° at Boulder in 2017. Sq conductivity is much weaker near sunset, so neither the dome's linear formula nor our daytime-derived ensemble comparator was scaled for this; our own amplitude range may be too high. (3) Coordinate label. The station magnetic latitudes we pre-registered (COI 43.7°, EBR 42.9°, SPT 42.4°, CLF 49.6°, Canary 33.2°, NGK 51.85°, HAD 53.6°, ESK 57.5°, LER 61.8°) are centered-dipole values (IGRF-14 epoch-2020 pole 80.65°N, 287.32°E), computed by us. Earlier text mislabelled them “CGM” and attributed them to an IAGA registry. Under the AACGM-v2 convention they are about 4°–12° lower (EBR 33.3°, SPT 31.1°, COI 32.0°, CLF 42.8°, HAD 46.7°, NGK 47.9°, ESK 51.9°, LER 57.5°; the AACGM value for the Canary station, 8.3°, is unreliable at that latitude and is left out). Hartland and Niemegk would then move inside the band, and Kim & Chang's abstract does not state which convention their 30°–50° band uses. Only Lerwick and Eskdalemuir fall outside the band under both conventions, so the discriminating signal rests on fewer stations than we claimed. The dipole-latitude correlation with geographic latitude (r = 0.991 over the eight European stations) is higher still under AACGM (r = 0.999), which makes the overlap between the two profiles worse. (4) Station labels and availability. The Canary station, labelled “SNK” in the dome's table, is INTERMAGNET GUI (Güímar). The dome's own station audit flags Coimbra as having no data and Lerwick as having 2023 data only. Coimbra could not be retrieved from INTERMAGNET for the evaluation. Given these limits, an outcome in which FSF tracks the residuals better than magnetic latitude would not by itself be evidence for dome physics, because both confounds favour FSF. We withdraw our earlier statement that such an outcome would leave “something non-trivial” to explain.

Post-event status (dated 2026-09-29). The eclipse occurred on 12 August 2026. Conditions: GFZ definitive Kp for 9–12 August peaked at 3o (11 August, 15–18 UTC). On the eclipse day it was 1+ at 15–18 UTC and 2+ at 18–21 UTC. The European partial phases ran from about 17:00 to 19:45 UTC; at eclipse maximum, eight of the nine dome-cited stations were in the 18–21 UTC slot (Kp 2+), and only Lerwick's maximum (17:58 UTC) fell in the 1+ slot (our JPL DE440s run). The dome's precondition failed on all three of its stated readings: “valid only if Kp < 2 on August 12, 2026”; “Kp < 2 entire Aug 9–12 window”; and, for its registered Ebro figure (PRED-095, −17.8 nT ±2 nT, registered 2026-04-04), “Requires Kp<2 within 3 hours of totality.” Ebro's totality was at 18:30 UTC, so that window covers the 1+, 2+ and 1o slots, and 2+ is not below 2. The dome's revised rule says “IF Kp ≥ 3 … not a falsification” and says nothing about 2 ≤ Kp < 3, which is where the eclipse fell. The dome's result: none posted, 48 days after the event. The dome's own plan was to “Pull INTERMAGNET + IGETS within 72h” and post “raw plots, r-values, asymmetry index, verdict — public record”, and it described the INTERMAGNET data as “available within 24h post-eclipse” (predictions.html). No result can be posted automatically: monitor.py domain #10 hardcodes observed = 'PENDING' and pass = None and has no code path that fetches INTERMAGNET data. The latest status_history.json record (2026-09-29T18:20Z) still reads PENDING at −49 days. Its stated falsification rule, “Fails if measured anomaly within ±3 nT of 0,” is one-sided: any |ΔB| above 3 nT counts as success. Our result: we set a +30-day evaluation date of about 11 September 2026 and missed it. A draft evaluation was run on 26 September and has been through four rounds of adversarial review; the latest (4 October) asked for a further targeted revision. We are not publishing magnetic verdicts here until that review is complete; the target for publishing the reviewed evaluation, with every registered claim scored, is 2026-10-31. Symmetry: both sides' magnetic claims were conditioned on Kp < 2, and that condition was not met. How both are labelled will be set by the same rule, in the reviewed results file. Our own errors so far: Erratum 1 (2026-09-27, OpenTimestamps-anchored) records two. Our frozen geometric claim B1-G-005 put Hartland's maximum obscuration at 88% ± 2 percentage points; the correct value is 94.4% at 18:15 UTC (JPL DE440s; timeanddate.com gives magnitude 0.947 for Bideford, 18 km east). B1-G-005 failed, and the failure is ours, not the standard model's; our §4.2.7 figures (88%, and a partial phase of “roughly 2 h 45 min” that is really 1 h 51 min) were corrected at the same time. Erratum 1 also records that our magnetic claim B1-M-001 cited its source paper under the wrong authors and title, and that its amplitude band is met on ordinary non-eclipse days (17 of 30 control days), so as registered it had little power to discriminate. Neither error bears on the dome-versus-globe shadow-geometry verdict, which rests on the path and size of totality.

Note: WIN-010, WIN-025, and WIN-068 all rest on the same Sq mechanism. Count inflation does not by itself refute any individual claim, but it is relevant context when the dome cites 69 confirmed predictions: three of them share one mechanism.

tldr_evidence.new: Eclipses cause small magnetic changes because the Moon's shadow weakens electric currents in the sunlit upper atmosphere, an effect Chapman worked out for the ionospheric current system in 1933 and that INTERMAGNET data confirmed statistically by 2018. At Boulder in 2017 the eclipse shows mainly in the north-south component; the vertical component the dome uses shows no detectable dip, and the dome's −18.22 nT figure is what Boulder's Z does on an ordinary August afternoon. The dome has since moved this WIN to a 2016 Pacific eclipse, which the same mechanism covers.

tldr_verdict.new: Standard physics predicts eclipse magnetic effects without dome parameters; the dome's station scaling is just the ratio of tan(latitude), and the signal's size is borrowed from 2017 Boulder data that the dome now calls storm-contaminated (Kp was at most 2o) yet still uses as calibration, and which ordinary quiet afternoons at Boulder match on the dome's own measure. On 12 August 2026 the dome's Kp precondition failed and it has posted no result; our own magnetic evaluation is late and still under review.

kernel_of_truth: The dome is right that eclipses produce measurable ground magnetic perturbations, right that geomagnetic quietness matters for detecting them, right that 2017-08-21 was disturbed in the morning (Kp 3o at 06-09 UT), and local Boulder variance is a reasonable detectability heuristic. Boulder's Z really did reach a low inside the 2017 eclipse window relative to that day's mean. Its FSF table genuinely follows from its own V12 flat triangulation, and pre-committing station-level numbers before 2026-08-12 was the right methodological move. None of that makes the signal a dome prediction: Boulder's Z reaches a similar low on quiet days with no eclipse, the eclipse effect that is present at Boulder is small and mostly in X, the magnitude is borrowed from an event the dome itself now disowns, the planetary Kp record gives no support to its storm label, its coverage inputs are wrong by up to about x2 against ephemeris, and its own precondition failed on the day.

anticipated_objections.objection: "You got both Kp values backwards and attacked us for the same error in WIN-025."
anticipated_objections.response: Conceded and corrected in-text with a dated correction note, using the same GFZ source as WIN-025. The corrected record hurts the dome more: its "quietest day" (2016, Kp 2o) was noisier on Kp than both "storm" days (2017 Kp 1+, 2024 Kp 0+), and it disowned 2017 while keeping it as calibration.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Quietness should be judged by local BOU variance, not planetary Kp."
anticipated_objections.response: Granted as a heuristic in the text. But the dome itself states its precondition in Kp, and if its variance is taken over the eclipse window it is confounded by Boulder local time (2016 at dusk vs 2017/2024 near noon). The local-time reading is flagged as our inference, not a verified fact.

anticipated_objections.objection: "By our pre-registered rule 2026 is not a falsification (Kp ≥ 2), and your frozen file says the same."
anticipated_objections.response: Agreed and stated symmetrically in the post-event paragraph. The text does not score the dome's escape clause against it. It records that the clause fired, that the dome's rule is silent on 2 ≤ Kp < 3, and that the dome's code cannot post any result, whereas we commit to publishing ours with misses.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Where is YOUR nine-station test? You promised it by 11 September."
anticipated_objections.response: Disclosed: we missed our own date; a draft exists and is in adversarial review; a public target date (2026-10-31) is given. No magnetic verdicts are claimed prematurely.
Confirmed by a non-DE421 source and self-disclosed as a failed claim, with the §4.2.7 duration error also corrected. It does not bear on the shadow-geometry verdict (path/size of totality).

Relabelled as computed centered-dipole; AACGM values shown; the discriminating set is narrowed to the two stations out-of-band under both conventions. Kim & Chang's convention is stated as unresolved rather than guessed.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Dropping the asymmetric-standard argument weakens the review."
anticipated_objections.response: It was factually wrong; keeping it would be the hypocrisy the defender describes. The replacement vise (disowned-as-evidence but retained-as-calibration, in the dome's own words on wins.html vs model.html vs monitor.py) is internal to the dome and needs none of our physics.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Your quiet-day reference is cherry-picked; pick other days and the eclipse dip appears."
anticipated_objections.response: The rule is stated and mechanical (five lowest-max-Kp days in 10-31 August, excluding the 21st), and the simplest check uses the dome's own chosen day: on 20 August, Z at 17:20 UT was 6.0 nT lower than during the eclipse. The published Meza et al. analysis, with its own five-quiet-day reference, also finds dZ positive at BOU.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Meza's numbers are read off a figure."
anticipated_objections.response: Yes, and the text says so. Their prose states the sign (dZ positive, lowest amplitude) without needing the figure; our own computation gives the magnitudes independently.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Chapman 1933 says the effect wasn't seen, so the globe had no mechanism."
anticipated_objections.response: Chapman 1933 predicted the effect from the mechanism and said the 1930s data could not yet settle it. Kim & Chang (2018) settled it statistically, and the dome's own predictions page heads its Tier 1 block 'Magnetic Signal (Globe-Compatible)'.
